title: L^2(μ) convergence of the cubic Wick term ∫ψ:u^3: along the regularization

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
**Step C2.** Expanding $\tfrac14(u+\psi)^4-\tfrac14u^4=\psi u^3+\tfrac32\psi^2u^2+\psi^3u+\tfrac14\psi^4$, the leading singular contribution to $V(u)-V_\psi(u)$ is the renormalized cubic $\int_{\mathbb{T}^3}\psi\,{:}u^3{:}$.

**Gap:** Prove a uniform-in-$N$ second-moment bound $\mathbb{E}_\mu\big[(\int\psi\,{:}u_N^3{:})^2\big]\le C\|\psi\|^2$ and a Cauchy estimate in $N$, giving convergence in $L^2(\mu)$ of $\int\psi\,{:}u_N^3{:}$ to a limit. Naive Gaussian Wick estimates do NOT apply because $\mu$ is non-Gaussian; the bound must use the stochastic-object estimates from the construction (Da Prato–Debussche / regularity structures / paracontrolled).

**Why hard:** ${:}u^3{:}$ for the $\Phi^4_3$ field is a genuinely singular object of regularity $-3/2-$; pairing against smooth $\psi$ recovers integrability but the moment bound under the *interacting* law requires the full second-order analysis.

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
**[Re: current `solution.tex`]** The current attempt keeps the **GFF Wick cube** $:\!v^3\!:$ as the cubic shift term (`eq:Qeps`,`eq:Qlim`) and argues convergence $\langle\psi_\epsilon,:\!v_\epsilon^3\!:\rangle\to\langle\psi,:\!v^3\!:\rangle$ **in $L^p(\nu)$** (`lem:W-converge`), then declares (Remark `rem:counterterm`) that "no new divergence arises." This is precisely the gap here:
- $L^p(\nu)$-convergence is not $L^2(\mu)$-convergence ($\mu\perp\nu$); "naive Gaussian Wick estimates do NOT apply because $\mu$ is non-Gaussian," as this issue states.
- Under $\mu$ the cubic generically needs an **additional $\psi$-dependent (log-divergent) counterterm**; the "no new divergence" claim is asserted without computing $\mathbb E_\mu[\langle\psi_\epsilon,:\!u_\epsilon^3\!:\rangle]$.

A fix must establish the $L^2(\mu)$ Cauchy bound using the interacting-field stochastic objects (Da Prato–Debussche / paracontrolled / regularity structures), and identify/subtract the $\mu$-side counterterm before the limit.
